# Hardy-Lorentz Spaces: Atomic Decomposition, Interpolation, and Operator Theory

## Introduction and Overview

This paper is devoted to a systematic study of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, a family of function spaces that generalize the classical Hardy spaces $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ by incorporating the refined scale of Lorentz space integrability. Specifically, we consider the full parameter range $0 < p \leq 1$ and $0 < q \leq \infty$, which includes the classical Hardy spaces as the special case $q = p$, while allowing for finer control over the distributional behavior of functions through the second parameter $q$. The investigation proceeds along four principal directions: atomic decomposition, interpolation theory, boundedness of singular integral operators, and the action of other significant operators arising in harmonic analysis.

## Atomic Decomposition

A central result of the paper is the establishment of an atomic decomposition theorem for elements of $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Following the classical paradigm initiated by Coifman and Latter for Hardy spaces, we show that every distribution $f \in H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ can be represented as a sum

$$f = \sum_{j} \lambda_j a_j$$

where each $a_j$ is a $(p,\infty)$-atom—supported in a cube (or ball), satisfying appropriate size and vanishing moment conditions dictated by the smoothness parameter $p$—and the coefficients $\{\lambda_j\}$ satisfy a Lorentz-space analog of the usual $\ell^p$ summability condition. This decomposition is shown to be essentially sharp, in the sense that the norm of $f$ in $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is equivalent to the infimum, over all such atomic representations, of the corresponding Lorentz-sequence-space quasi-norm of the coefficients. The atomic characterization provides an indispensable tool for the subsequent analysis, as it reduces many questions about arbitrary elements of $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ to verification on the level of individual atoms.

## Interpolation Properties

Building upon the atomic decomposition, the paper investigates the interpolation properties of the scale $\{H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\}$. We demonstrate that these spaces arise naturally as real interpolation spaces between classical Hardy spaces $H^{p_0}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $H^{p_1}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, in analogy with the classical Lorentz space interpolation results for $L^p$ spaces due to Calderón. More precisely, results of the form

$$\left(H^{p_0}(\mathbb{R}^n), H^{p_1}(\mathbb{R}^n)\right)_{\theta, q} = H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$$

are established, where $0 < p_0 < p_1 \leq 1$, $0 < \theta < 1$, and $\frac{1}{p} = \frac{1-\theta}{p_0} + \frac{\theta}{p_1}$. These interpolation identities not only clarify the structural position of $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ within the broader landscape of function spaces, but also furnish an efficient method for deriving boundedness results for sublinear or linear operators: it suffices to verify appropriate estimates on the endpoint Hardy spaces $H^{p_0}$ and $H^{p_1}$, and interpolation then automatically yields boundedness on the intermediate Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}$ for all admissible $q$.

## Boundedness of Singular Integral Operators

A significant portion of the paper is dedicated to analyzing the action of singular integral operators—including Calderón-Zygmund operators and their variants—on the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Using the atomic decomposition established earlier, we prove that operators satisfying standard Calderón-Zygmund kernel conditions, together with the requisite cancellation or vanishing moment properties, map $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ boundedly into itself (or into an appropriate target Hardy-Lorentz space) for the full range $0 < p \leq 1$, $0 < q \leq \infty$. The proof strategy follows the standard reduction to atoms: one first verifies that the image of an atom under the singular integral operator possesses a suitable molecular decomposition or satisfies appropriate size and decay estimates, and then assembles these atomic estimates into a global bound using the Lorentz-sequence-space summability of the atomic coefficients. This yields sharp $H^{p,q} \to H^{p,q}$ and $H^{p,q} \to L^{p,q}$ type boundedness results that extend and unify various results previously known for classical Hardy spaces and for Lorentz spaces separately.

## Action of Related Operators

Finally, the paper extends this analysis to other operators of interest in harmonic analysis and partial differential equations, including maximal functions (such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and its grand or radial variants used in the very characterization of $H^{p,q}$), fractional integral operators (Riesz potentials), and pseudo-differential operators of appropriate order. For each such operator, we establish mapping properties between Hardy-Lorentz spaces, or between a Hardy-Lorentz space and a Lorentz space, again relying crucially on the atomic decomposition and, where relevant, on the interpolation results developed earlier. Together, these results demonstrate that the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ constitute a natural and robust framework for harmonic analysis, fully compatible with the principal tools—atomic decomposition, interpolation, and operator estimates—that have proven so effective in the classical Hardy space theory.

## Conclusion

Taken together, the results of this paper provide a comprehensive and self-contained treatment of the Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $0 < p \leq 1$ and $0 < q \leq \infty$. The atomic decomposition serves as the foundational tool, from which both the interpolation theory and the operator-theoretic results are derived. These findings not only deepen our understanding of the fine structure of Hardy-type spaces but also provide new tools applicable to problems in partial differential equations, approximation theory, and other areas where refined integrability estimates are essential.

The theory of Hardy spaces $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for $0 < p \leq 1$ has played a fundamental role in harmonic analysis since the pioneering work of Stein, Weiss, and Fefferman. These spaces serve as natural substitutes for $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ when $p \leq 1$, since $L^p$ fails to interact well with classical operators such as the Hilbert transform and Riesz transforms in this range. The real-variable theory of Hardy spaces, developed extensively by Coifman, Latter, and others, established the atomic decomposition as a cornerstone technique: every element of $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ can be written as a sum of simple building blocks called atoms, each supported on a cube and satisfying moment cancellation conditions.

A natural and important refinement of this theory involves considering Lorentz-space variants of Hardy spaces. The Lorentz spaces $L^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ provide a finer scale of function spaces than the Lebesgue spaces $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, allowing one to distinguish between functions with the same $L^p$-norm but different distributional behavior. The Hardy-Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, obtained by imposing a Lorentz-space condition on the maximal function (or grand maximal function) associated to tempered distributions, generalize both the classical Hardy spaces $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (recovered when $q = p$) and the Lorentz spaces $L^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ (for $p > 1$).

This paper is devoted to a systematic study of $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for the full range $0 < p \leq 1$ and $0 < q \leq \infty$. 1. **Interpolation**: How do Hardy-Lorentz spaces behave under real and complex interpolation, both among themselves and with related classical spaces?

2. **Boundedness of operators**: Under what conditions do classical singular integral operators, and more general operators satisfying suitable smoothness and cancellation conditions, act boundedly on $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$?

## 2. Preliminaries and Definitions

### 2.1 Lorentz Spaces

Recall that for a measurable function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, the decreasing rearrangement $f^*$ is defined by
$$
f^*(t) = \inf\{\lambda > 0 : |\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |f(x)| > \lambda\}| \leq t\}.
$$
For $0 < p < \infty$ and $0 < q \leq \infty$, the Lorentz space $L^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ consists of all measurable $f$ for which the quasi-norm
$$
\|f\|_{L^{p,q}} = 
\begin{cases}
\left(\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \left(t^{1/p} f^*(t)\right)^q \frac{dt}{t}\right)^{1/q}, & 0 < q < \infty, \\
\sup_{t>0} t^{1/p} f^*(t), & q = \infty,
\end{cases}
$$
is finite. When $q = p$, this reduces to the usual Lebesgue norm $\|f\|_{L^p}$. The parameter $q$ provides a secondary index controlling the fine structure of the decreasing rearrangement, with smaller $q$ corresponding to stronger integrability conditions.

### 2.2 The Hardy-Lorentz Spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$

Let $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ denote the Schwartz class and $\mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n)$ its dual. Fix $N \in \mathbb{N}$ sufficiently large (depending on $p$) and define, for $\phi \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, the grand maximal function
$$
M_N f(x) = \sup_{\varphi \in \mathcal{F}_N} \sup_{t > 0} |(f * \varphi_t)(x)|,
$$
where $\mathcal{F}_N$ is the set of Schwartz functions $\varphi$ with seminorms bounded by $1$ up to order $N$, and $\varphi_t(x) = t^{-n}\varphi(x/t)$.

**Definition.** For $0 < p \leq 1$ and $0 < q \leq \infty$, the Hardy-Lorentz space $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is defined as
$$
H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n) = \{ f \in \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^n) : M_N f \in L^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)\},
$$
with quasi-norm $\|f\|_{H^{p,q}} = \|M_N f\|_{L^{p,q}}$.

When $q = p$, this coincides with the classical Hardy space $H^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The scale $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ thus interpolates, in a suitable sense, between different classical Hardy spaces and captures finer distinctions in the decay and cancellation properties of distributions.

The atomic decomposition is the key structural tool of this paper. We say that a function $a$ supported in a cube $Q \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ is a $(p, r)$-atom (for $1 < r \leq \infty$) if:

- (Size condition) $\|a\|_{L^r} \leq |Q|^{1/r - 1/p}$;

# The Hardy-Lorentz Spaces: A Bridge Between Analysis and Function Theory

The mathematical landscape of function spaces owes much to two remarkable contributors: G.H. Hardy and Hendrik Lorentz, whose names have become intertwined in the theory of Hardy-Lorentz spaces—a sophisticated generalization that has proven indispensable in harmonic analysis and complex function theory.

## Historical Foundations

G.H. Hardy, the eminent British mathematician of the early twentieth century, established what we now call Hardy spaces (Hp spaces) through his investigations into the boundary behavior of analytic functions. Working primarily on the unit disc and upper half-plane, Hardy demonstrated how functions satisfying certain integrability conditions on circles of varying radii could be understood through their boundary values, creating a powerful framework connecting complex analysis with real-variable methods.

Hendrik Lorentz, though primarily celebrated for his contributions to theoretical physics—particularly the Lorentz transformations fundamental to special relativity—also left an indelible mark on mathematical analysis through the Lorentz spaces he introduced. These spaces, denoted L(p,q), refine the classical Lp spaces by introducing an additional parameter that allows for finer control over function behavior, distinguishing between functions that might have identical Lp norms but different distributional characteristics.

## The Synthesis: Hardy-Lorentz Spaces

The marriage of these two theoretical frameworks produces Hardy-Lorentz spaces, typically denoted Hp,q, which combine the analytic structure of Hardy spaces with the refined integrability scale of Lorentz spaces. This synthesis offers several advantages:

**Finer Gradations**: While classical Hardy spaces provide a discrete scale indexed by p, Hardy-Lorentz spaces introduce continuous refinement through the second parameter q, allowing mathematicians to distinguish between spaces that would otherwise be conflated.

**Interpolation Properties**: These spaces exhibit excellent behavior under interpolation, making them valuable tools for proving boundedness results for various operators, including the Hilbert transform, maximal functions, and singular integral operators.

**Applications in Harmonic Analysis**: Hardy-Lorentz spaces have found applications in the study of Fourier series convergence, the theory of singular integrals, and the analysis of martingales, extending classical results to broader contexts.

## Contemporary Relevance

Modern research continues to explore Hardy-Lorentz spaces in various settings, including several complex variables, weighted function spaces, and non-commutative analysis. The interplay between Hardy's original insights into analytic function behavior and Lorentz's refinement of measure-theoretic function spaces exemplifies how seemingly disparate mathematical traditions can combine to create richer, more nuanced theoretical frameworks.

This convergence of ideas—one rooted in complex analysis, the other in real analysis and measure theory—demonstrates the deeply interconnected nature of mathematical disciplines, where tools developed for different purposes often find unexpected synthesis in solving broader classes of problems.

We present a systematic study of the Hardy–Lorentz spaces $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for the full range of indices $0 < p \le 1$ and $0 < q \le \infty$, which arise as natural refinements of the classical Hardy spaces $H^p$ obtained by replacing the Lebesgue norm in the boundary decomposition with the Lorentz quasi-norm $L^{p,q}$. $$

As applications, the atomic decomposition is used to establish sharp boundedness criteria for sublinear operators $T$ satisfying uniform size and cancellation estimates on atoms: if $T$ maps $(p,\infty)$-atoms into functions uniformly bounded in $H^{p,q}$ (or $L^{p,q}$), then $T$ extends to a bounded operator on the whole space $H^{p,q}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. This criterion is applied to Calderón–Zygmund singular integral operators, fractional integral (Riesz potential) operators between Hardy–Lorentz spaces of different smoothness, and Fourier multiplier operators of Hörmander–Mikhlin type, yielding endpoint mapping properties $T: H^{p,q} \to H^{p,q}$ and $T: H^{p,q}\to L^{p,q}$ that sharpen known $L^p$ and $H^p$ estimates by capturing finer integrability information encoded in the secondary parameter $q$. Boundedness of maximal truncated singular integrals and commutators with $\mathrm{BMO}$ functions is also discussed within this framework.

**Keywords:** Hardy–Lorentz space, atomic decomposition, real interpolation, Calderón–Zygmund operator, maximal function, Lorentz sequence space.
